summary:
ASTRIX Saudi Analogs is an interactive web platform that links Saudi Arabian terrain to the environments where real space missions failed, and shows where those failures can be tested on Earth before launch.

What we developed: a map of Saudi sites backed by published evidence (lava fields, impact craters, dune seas) plus clearly marked candidates that still need verification; a 3D terrain tour built from NASA SRTM elevation that shows the same ground as Earth, Moon or Mars; mission replays such as Curiosity and Surveyor 1; and a planner that matches a space system and environmental stresses to a Saudi site and season.

How it addresses the challenge: it identifies and characterizes terrestrial analogs for lunar and Martian conditions using NASA and open data, and presents them as a map, a 3D visualization and a test-planning tool.

Why it matters: dust, loose sand, sharp rock and cold nights have ended or crippled missions for decades, and an Earth test only helps if the site reproduces the right combination of conditions.

What makes it special: we start from the mission failure, not from the terrain. Every site carries an evidence grade, unverified candidates are labelled, and we state what Earth cannot reproduce, such as gravity and atmosphere.
details:
What it does and how it works

ASTRIX Saudi Analogs is an interactive web platform that links Saudi Arabian terrain to the environments where real space missions failed, and shows where those conditions can be tested on Earth before launch. Users can browse Saudi sites with an evidence grade, explore each site in 3D as Earth, Moon or Mars, replay mission failures (Opportunity, InSight, Spirit and Curiosity), find a site by destination, terrain and test type, and use a planner that matches a space system and environmental stresses to a site and season.

Our workflow: Discover under-documented craters, sinkholes and cavities from literature and imagery; Measure diameter, depth and slope from elevation data; Compare them with documented lunar and Martian features; Recommend a site and season for a given system and failure.

Benefits and intended impact

Engineers usually test hardware at a few well-known places. We help them find additional, closer test sites, and we open Saudi Arabia as a source of under-studied analog terrain. Each site shows an evidence grade. Sites without published evidence are labelled as candidates that still need verification.

Tools, languages and data

Built as a single-page web application with HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework), Three.js (WebGL) for 3D terrain, WebXR for the headset preview, and Leaflet for the interactive map. Hosted on GitHub Pages.

NASA data: NASA GIBS imagery layers (VIIRS true color, MODIS land surface temperature, ASTER GDEM shaded relief). Elevation for the 3D terrain comes from AWS Terrain Tiles, a composite dataset that includes NASA SRTM. High-resolution imagery is from Esri World Imagery (not NASA, credited separately). Next steps: NASADEM, NASA POWER, MERRA-2, LROC and HiRISE.

What makes it creative

We start from the mission failure, not from the terrain. The same ground can be viewed as Earth, Moon or Mars side by side, with a movable Sun, and each failure is linked to a place where it can be tested.

Factors we considered

• Evidence: every site carries a grade from published studies. Candidates without published evidence are marked.

• Limits of an analog: gravity (9.8 vs 1.6 and 3.7 m/s²), atmosphere and radiation differ. The Moon and Mars views re-color and re-light the same Earth terrain, so they are visualizations, not proof of equivalence.

• Prototype values: the test-planner match values and readiness scores are indicative values assigned by our team. They are not computed from NASA measurements yet.

• Data resolution: roughly 30 m elevation data can miss small pits, and route slopes are approximate.

• Seasons: indicative until checked against NASA POWER records.

• Safety: all work was done remotely from data and imagery.

• Testing: weather data cannot prove material durability. Real tests need samples and instruments.
